p.seg: The Great Way is formless,
but objects have names.
Names are what rectify forms.
Since forms are rectified through names,
names must not be erroneous.
Thus Confucius said:
"Must we not rectify names?
If names are not rectified,
then speech will not flow smoothly."
The Great Way is not named,
but all entities must have names.
Born from the unnamed,
all forms naturally attain their squares and circles;
names arise from squares and circles,
thus all names obtain what they designate.
When governing through the Great Way,
names, laws, Confucianism, and Mohism naturally become obsolete;
when governing through names, laws, Confucianism, and Mohism,
one cannot depart from the Way.
Laozi said:
"The Way is the mystery of all things,
the treasure of good people,
and what is preserved by those who are not good."
Those who govern through the Way
are called good people;
those who rely on names, laws, Confucianism, and Mohism
are called not good people.
Between good and not good people,
the distinction in names daily widens,
yet cannot be fully grasped through examination.
When the Way is insufficient for governance, laws are used;
when laws are insufficient, methods are used;
when methods are insufficient, authority is used;
when authority is insufficient, power is used.
When power is used, it reverts to authority;
when authority is used, it reverts to methods;
when methods are used, they revert to laws;
when laws are used, they revert to the Way;
when the Way is used, there is non-action and self-governance.
Thus when exhausted, it returns to the end,
and returning to the end means reverting to the beginning;
beginning and end follow each other,
without limit.
What has form must have a name,
but what has a name may not necessarily have form.
Having form without a name
does not necessarily lose the reality of square, circle, white, or black;
having a name without form
requires examining its discrepancies through the name.
Thus names are also used to examine forms,
forms to determine names,
names to determine affairs,
and affairs to examine names.
By investigating their reasons,
the principles of forms, names, and things
cannot be hidden.
Names have three categories,
laws have four manifestations.
The first is names for objects,
such as square, circle, white, black;
the second is names for praise and blame,
such as good, evil, noble, base;
the third is names for descriptions,
such as wise, foolish, love, hate.
The first is unchanging laws,
such as ruler and subject, superior and inferior;
the second is laws for unifying customs,
such as ability and incompetence, similarity and difference;
the third is laws for governing the masses,
such as rewards, commendations, punishments, and penalties;
the fourth is laws for standardization,
such as pitch-pipes, measurements, weights, and capacities.
Methods are what the ruler uses secretly,
and subordinates must not recklessly spy on;
power is the sharp tool for establishing laws,
and subordinates must not recklessly act upon.
If the ruler has methods
but allows subordinates to spy on them,
these are not profound methods;
if he has power
but allows subordinates to wield it,
this is not weighty power.
The essential point lies first in rectifying names and distinctions,
preventing mutual infringement and confusion.
Only then can methods be kept secret and power monopolized.
Names are what name forms,
forms are what correspond to names.
However, if forms do not rectify names,
and names do not rectify forms,
then forms and names
are clearly distinct,
cannot be confused,
yet cannot exist without each other.
Without names, the Great Way remains unnamed;
with names, they are used to rectify forms.
Now all things exist,
but without naming them correctly, there will be chaos;
all names are listed,
but without forms corresponding to them, there will be discord.
Therefore, forms and names must be rectified.
Good names designate good,
evil names designate evil,
thus good has good names,
evil has evil names.
Sage, worthy, benevolent, wise
designate the good;
stubborn, deceitful,凶, foolish
designate the evil.
Now using the names of sage, worthy, benevolent, wise
to seek their reality,
one may not fully grasp them;
using the names of stubborn, deceitful,凶, foolish
to seek their reality,
one may also not fully grasp them.
If good and evil were clearly distinguished,
even without fully grasping the reality of things,
one need not worry about errors.
Thus it is said:
"Names must be distinguished."
Names and designations
are what distinguish this from that and examine emptiness and reality.
From ancient times to the present,
none have not succeeded by using this
and failed by using that.
Failure arises from confusion of names and distinctions,
success from clarity of names and distinctions.
Now drawing close to the worthy and keeping distant from the unworthy,
rewarding the good and punishing the evil.
The names of worthy, unworthy, good, evil
should belong to them;
the designations of closeness, distance, reward, punishment
should belong to me.
Between me and them,
there is again a single name.
This is the clarity of names,
naming the worthy and unworthy as closeness and distance,
naming the good and evil as reward and punishment.
Combining their and my designations without distinction
is the confusion of names.
Thus it is said:
"Names and designations
must be examined."
There is a saying:
"Good ox."
And also:
"Must be examined."
"Good" is the universal designation of things,
"ox" is the fixed form of a thing,
applying universal designations to fixed forms
is limitless.
If one speaks of "good horse,"
then it is again connected to horse.
Thus what "good" applies to
has no fixed direction.
If one speaks of "good person,"
then it belongs to person.
Thus "good" is not person,
person is not "good";
then the names "good ox," "good horse," "good person" are naturally distinct.
Therefore it is said:
"Names and distinctions must not be confused."
The five colors, five tones, five odors, and five flavors,
these four categories in total,
naturally exist between heaven and earth,
without intending to be used by humans.
Humans inevitably use them,
each having their own preferences and aversions throughout life,
yet unable to distinguish their proper designations and roles,
which designations should belong to them,
and which should belong to us.
I love white and hate black,
resonate with shāng and reject zhǐ,
prefer gamy smells and dislike burnt odors,
crave sweetness and reject bitterness.
White, black, shāng, zhǐ, gamy, burnt, sweet, bitter -
these are their names;
love, hate, resonate, reject, prefer, dislike, crave, reject -
these are my distinctions.
By establishing these names and distinctions,
all affairs become orderly.
Thus people use measures to determine length,
use containers to receive quantity,
use scales to balance weight,
use pitch pipes to harmonize clarity and turbidity,
use names to verify truth and falsehood,
use laws to regulate order and chaos,
use simplicity to manage complexity and confusion,
use ease to control difficulty and danger.
All things return to unity,
all standards conform to law.
Returning to unity is the ultimate simplicity,
conforming to law is the ultimate ease.
In this way,
the stubborn, garrulous, deaf, and blind
can achieve governance equal to the perceptive, wise, sharp-eared, and clear-sighted.
No one in the world can master all skills,
to demand complete capability from one person -
wouldn't even sages and worthies find this difficult?
Suppose one person could handle all worldly affairs,
could manage all directions appropriately,
balancing far and near, slow and fast -
there would inevitably be areas where they fall short.
If there are shortcomings,
governance becomes deficient.
Complete governance without deficiency
requires that great and small, much and little,
each fulfills its proper role,
with farmers, merchants, craftsmen, and officials not changing their occupations,
and experienced farmers, veteran merchants, skilled craftsmen, and seasoned officials all preserved.
Then what need is there for those above to act?
Therefore, principles that don't benefit governance -
the noble person doesn't speak them;
abilities that don't benefit affairs -
the noble person doesn't exercise them.
The noble person doesn't enjoy speaking,
but when it benefits governance,
cannot avoid speaking;
the noble person doesn't enjoy acting,
but when it benefits affairs,
cannot avoid acting.
Thus what they speak never goes beyond names, laws, authority, and methods;
what they do never goes beyond farming, military formations.
They simply attend to essential matters,
hence the enlightened ruler doesn't act unnecessarily.
Principles beyond governance -
petty people inevitably discuss;
abilities beyond affairs -
petty people inevitably exercise.
They know speaking damages governance,
yet cannot refrain from speaking;
they know ability damages affairs,
yet cannot refrain from acting.
Thus what they speak
reaches extremes in debating Confucian and Mohist rights and wrongs;
what they do
reaches extremes in stubborn, false, biased, and resistant behavior,
merely seeking fame,
hence the wise ruler punishes them.
An ancient saying states:
"Not knowing doesn't harm the noble person,
knowing doesn't benefit the petty person.
A craftsman's lack of knowledge doesn't harm his skill,
a noble person's lack of knowledge doesn't harm governance."
This is indeed true.
Doing good
in a way that others cannot follow -
this is solitary goodness.
Being skillful
in a way that others cannot emulate -
this is solitary skill.
This doesn't exhaust the principles of goodness and skill.
Doing good that everyone can practice,
being skillful that everyone can emulate -
this is the goodness of goodness, the skill of skill.
What we value in the sage's governance
isn't his solitary governing,
but his ability to govern together with everyone;
what we value in the craftsman's skill
isn't his solitary skill,
but his ability to be skillful together with everyone.
People nowadays
seek to be uniquely virtuous in conduct,
uniquely capable in affairs,
uniquely outstanding in debate,
uniquely surpassing in courage.
Solitary virtue
cannot accomplish transformation;
solitary capability
cannot handle all affairs;
outstanding debate
cannot serve for household instruction;
surpassing courage
cannot be used in battle formations.
These four things
are the sources of chaos.
Therefore, the sage employs the Way to level risks,
establishes laws to regulate differences,
ensuring the worthy and foolish don't reject each other,
the capable and incompetent don't abandon each other.
When capable and incompetent don't abandon each other,
they achieve equal merit;
when worthy and foolish don't reject each other,
they achieve equal consideration.
This is the method of perfect governance.
When names are settled,
things don't compete;
when distinctions are clear,
selfishness doesn't operate.
Things not competing
doesn't mean they lack intention -
because names are settled,
they have nowhere to apply their intention;
selfishness not operating
doesn't mean there are no desires -
because distinctions are clear,
they have nowhere to apply their desires.
Thus intention and desire exist in everyone,
yet achieving unity of intention and absence of desire
comes from having methods to control them.
Tián Pián said:
"All scholars under heaven dwell within their gates and courtyards,
serving their wives and children,
yet necessarily seek office at feudal lords' courts -
profit draws them.
Serving at feudal lords' courts,
all aim to become ministers and officials,
but don't aspire to become feudal lords themselves -
names limit them."
Péng Méng said:
"Pheasants and hares in the wilds -
everyone chases them,
because distinctions aren't settled.
Chickens and pigs filling the markets -
no one has designs on them,
because distinctions are settled."
When things are excessive,
benevolence and wisdom become constrained;
when distinctions are settled,
greed and meanness don't contend.
The circle's turning
isn't that it can turn and therefore turns,
but that it cannot but turn;
the square's staying
isn't that it can stay and therefore stays,
but that it cannot but stay.
Following the circle's natural turning,
make it unable to stop;
following the square's natural staying,
make it unable to turn -
why worry about things losing their distinctions?
Thus following the worthy person's usefulness,
make them unable not to be used;
following the foolish person's uselessness,
make them unable to be used.
Being used or not used
doesn't depend on my using them,
but by following their usefulness or uselessness,
I naturally obtain their use.
Why worry about things causing chaos?
Things cannot make themselves capable,
cannot know themselves through knowing.
The wise aren't wise because they can be wise,
the foolish aren't foolish because they can be foolish.
They become wise and foolish
not because they can prefer and therefore prefer,
not because they can dislike and therefore dislike.
If they cannot make themselves capable,
cannot know themselves through knowing,
then why value wisdom and preference?
Why disdain foolishness and ugliness?
Then the wise cannot boast over the foolish,
the preferred cannot ridicule the ugly.
When the Way prevails in the world,
the poor and lowly do not complain,
the rich and noble are not arrogant,
the foolish and weak do not feel intimidated,
and the wise and brave do not oppress others,
because everyone is settled in their proper roles.
When laws prevail in the world,
the poor and lowly dare not complain against the rich and noble,
the rich and noble dare not oppress the poor and lowly,
the foolish and weak dare not hope to match the wise and brave,
and the wise and brave dare not despise the foolish and weak.
This shows how law falls short of the Way.
What the world values,
and everyone values alike,
is called custom;
what ministers employ,
and everyone employs alike,
is called material goods.
If one goes against people,
custom will not accept it;
if one envies the multitude,
custom will collectively reject it.
Thus, though hearts differ,
actions appear uniform;
though preferences vary,
resources used must be the same.
This is what custom standardizes,
and what material goods adorn.
Therefore, what is standardized must be carefully considered,
and what is adorned must be carefully chosen.
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí loved purple robes,
and within his borders, no other colors were sold;
King Zhuāng of Chǔ admired slender waists,
and the whole state had a starved look.
What those above use to lead those below
is the source of order or chaos.
So if customs become corrupt,
governance must correct them;
if material goods become excessive,
regulations must restrain them.
Those burdened by custom
and adorned by material goods
cannot be engaged in governance.
In the past, the state of Jìn suffered from extravagance,
and Duke Wén corrected it with frugality,
wearing no double silks,
eating no dual meats.
Before long,
everyone wore coarse cloth
and ate unpolished rice.
King Gōujiàn of Yuè sought revenge against Wú,
desiring his people's courage,
and on the road, he saluted an angry frog.
After several years,
young and old among the people,
when facing the enemy,
would not avoid boiling water or fire.
The difficulty for those in high positions
is thus demonstrated.
The sage kings knew that human emotions are easily stirred,
so they created music to harmonize them,
and established rites to regulate them.
Those below cannot exercise their selfish desires,
hence rites and music prevail alone.
When rites and music prevail alone,
selfish desires gradually cease;
when selfish desires cease,
encountering the worthy or the foolish becomes equal.
If order depends on encountering the worthy,
and chaos on encountering the foolish,
then order and chaos hinge on worthiness or foolishness,
not on rites and music.
Thus, the methods of the sages
would perish with the sage rulers.
The laws of a well-ordered age,
if discarded after a change of era,
lead to more chaos and less order.
With more chaos and less order,
the worthy are not esteemed,
and the foolish are not despised.
Holding fame and position,
even if unworthy,
one need not worry that others will not be close;
in poverty and lowliness,
one need not worry that others will not be distant.
Closeness and distance depend on power and profit,
not on unworthiness or virtue.
I dare not claim this as heavenly principle or natural terrain.
Now, between heaven and earth,
the unworthy are truly many,
and the virtuous truly few.
The tendency toward profit
is especially strong in the unworthy;
the sense of shame
is more common in the virtuous.
Using ritual and righteousness to attract the virtuous,
the number gained
is less than one in ten thousand;
using fame and profit to attract the unworthy,
the number gained
is everywhere.
Hence it is said:
"Ritual and righteousness make the gentleman,
but the gentleman does not necessarily need them;
fame and profit control the petty person,
and the petty person cannot be without them."
Rewards and punishments
are the ruler's affairs;
fulfilling duties competently
is the minister's work.
The ruler assesses achievements for promotion or demotion,
hence there are rewards and punishments;
ministers are cautious in their responsibilities,
hence there is fulfillment of duties.
The ruler should not engage in ministers' work,
and ministers should not encroach on the ruler's affairs.
When superiors and subordinates do not encroach on each other,
it is called correct naming.
With correct naming, laws follow smoothly.
Engage with all things to distinguish them,
separate the world to avoid confusion,
face insult without feeling disgraced,
face praise without becoming proud,
prohibit violence and cease warfare,
and rescue the world from conflict.
These are the virtues of a benevolent ruler,
fit to be sovereign.
Maintain duties without disorder,
be cautious in responsibilities without selfishness,
unite in hunger and fullness,
share considerations of praise and blame,
neither forget rewards,
nor resent punishments.
These are the principles of those below,
fit to be people.
In the world, some gain reality through names,
and some lose reality through names.
King Xuān, fond of archery,
liked others saying he could use a strong bow,
though in reality he used no more than two dàn,
and showed it to his attendants,
who all tried to draw it,
stopping at half-draw,
and all said:
"No less than nine dàn—
who but the great king could use this?"
King Xuān was pleased.
Thus, King Xuān used no more than three dàn,
yet all his life believed it was nine.
Three dàn was the reality,
nine dàn was the name.
King Xuān delighted in the name and lost the reality.
In Qí, there was a Lord Huáng,
who favored humility.
He had two daughters,
both of stunning beauty.
Because of their beauty,
he often modestly disparaged them,
considering them ugly.
The reputation for ugliness spread far,
and they passed marriageable age with no proposals in the state.
A widower in Wèi
boldly married one,
and she was indeed stunningly beautiful.
Then it was said:
"Lord Huáng loves humility,
so he slandered his daughters.
If not beautiful, they must be beautiful."
Thereupon, people vied to court them,
and they were also stunningly beautiful.
Stunning beauty was the reality,
ugliness was the name.
This is gaining reality by going against the name.
A man from Chǔ carrying a pheasant
was asked by a passerby:
"What bird is this?"
The carrier deceived him, saying:
"It is a fènghuáng."
The passerby said:
"I have heard of the fènghuáng,
and now I see one truly.
Will you sell it?"
The man replied:
"Yes."
The price was ten pieces of gold,
but he refused to pay.
Upon offering double,
the carrier sold it to him.
Intending to present it to the King of Chǔ,
the bird died overnight.
The passerby did not regret the gold spent,
but only lamented failing to offer it to the King of Chǔ.
The story spread among the people,
all believing it was a true fènghuáng,
valuing the intention to present it.
Thus, the King of Chǔ heard of it.
Touched by his desire to offer it to himself,
the king summoned and richly rewarded him,
exceeding the bird's price tenfold.
A farmer from Wèi, while plowing in the field,
found a precious jade a foot in diameter.
Unaware it was jade,
he told his neighbor.
The neighbor secretly plotted to acquire it,
telling him:
"It is an ominous stone.
Keeping it
will bring no benefit to your family;
better return it."
Though the farmer doubted,
he still took it home.
Placing it under the eaves,
that night the jade glowed,
illuminating the entire room.
The farmer and his family were terrified,
and he reported it again to the neighbor.
Who said:
"This is a sign of evil;
discard it quickly,
and calamity may be averted."
So he hastily threw it into a distant field.
Soon after, the neighbor stole it
and presented it to the King of Wèi.
The king summoned a jade artisan to examine it.
The artisan gazed at it,
bowed twice and stood,
daring to congratulate the king on the jade:
"Your Majesty has obtained a treasure of the world,
such as I have never seen."
The king inquired its value,
and the artisan said:
"It is priceless.
Even a metropolis of five cities
is worth only a glimpse."
The king immediately rewarded the presenter with a thousand pieces of gold
and granted him a perpetual salary of a senior official.
Throughout the world, right and wrong exist everywhere,
which I dare not deny;
what is right is often right,
and what is wrong is often wrong,
which I also believe.
Yet, though right is often right,
sometimes it is not applied;
though wrong is often wrong,
sometimes it must be practiced.
Thus, applying right may lead to loss,
while practicing wrong may bring gain.
The principles of right and wrong differ,
alternating in rise and decline,
reversed for our use—
then where does right or wrong truly lie?
Observing the successes of Yáo, Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ,
whether through compliance or defiance,
seizing the moment brings prosperity.
The failures of Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì,
whether right or wrong,
losing the moment leads to ruin.
The same applies to the five hegemons.
When the Duke of Sòng battled the Chǔ at Hóng,
his son Mùyí said:
"The Chǔ are many, we are few;
I suggest we attack before they fully cross."
The Duke replied:
"No!
I have heard one should not drum against an unformed line.
Though I am but a remnant of the fallen,
I dare not do this."
They were defeated,
and the Chǔ captured the Duke of Sòng.
When the people of Qí assassinated Duke Xiāng,
they set up Gōngsūn Wúzhī.
Zhàohū and Yíwú escorted Prince Jiǔ to Lǔ,
while Bào Shūyá escorted Prince Xiǎobái to Jǔ.
Soon after, Wúzhī was killed,
and the two princes contended for the throne.
Jiǔ was the rightful heir;
but Xiǎobái entered first,
so the people of Qí established him.
Later, he had the people of Lǔ kill Jiǔ,
Zhàohū died for it,
and he summoned Yíwú to be his minister.
Duke Wén of Jìn, due to Lí Jī's slander, was exiled for nineteen years.
When Duke Huì died,
he bribed Qín to return to his state,
killed Prince Huái, and established himself.
One ruler acted rightly,
yet was captured;
two rulers acted wrongly,
but achieved hegemony.
If one is right but the whole world deems it wrong,
one may not know one's own rightness;
if one is wrong but the whole world deems it right,
one may not know one's own wrongness.
Thus, right and wrong are determined by public opinion,
not by individual insight.
So, opposing the masses is wrong,
while conforming to them is right.
Therefore, a ruler holding power and influence,
positioned where he is deemed right,
cannot be faulted by others.
In repose, all honor him;
in action, all follow him;
in speech, all trust him;
in conduct, all emulate him;
thus he remains above all,
governing the multitude.
There are three causes of national disorder:
famine dispersing the people,
with no food to gather them,
leads to disorder;
governing without laws,
leads to disorder;
having laws but not enforcing them,
leads to disorder;
with food to gather the people,
and laws that are enforced,
for a state not to be orderly,
has never happened.
Benevolence, righteousness, ritual, music, names, laws, punishments, and rewards—
these eight
are the methods by which the Five Emperors and Three Kings governed the world.
Thus, benevolence guides them,
righteousness suits them,
ritual enacts them,
music harmonizes them,
names rectify them,
laws standardize them,
punishments intimidate them,
rewards encourage them.
For benevolence widely bestows on all,
but also breeds partiality;
righteousness establishes integrity,
but also fosters hypocrisy;
ritual promotes respect,
but also induces laziness;
music harmonizes emotions,
but also leads to excess;
names rectify hierarchy,
but also cause arrogance and usurpation;
laws unify differences,
but also disrupt roles;
punishments intimidate the defiant,
but also breed violence;
rewards encourage loyalty and ability,
but also incite base strife.
All these eight methods,
not hidden from people and ever present in the world,
were not prominent only in the times of Yáo and Tāng,
nor absent in the courts of Jié and Zhòu.
Used correctly,
they bring order to the world;
misused,
they bring chaos.
Beyond this,
even if one encompasses heaven and earth,
and embraces all things,
outside the way of governance,
they are not what the multitude relies on,
and the sages set aside without mention.
There are six signs indicating the survival or demise of a state:
a declining state,
a perishing state,
a flourishing state,
a strong state,
a well-governed state,
and a chaotic state.
When speaking of chaotic and perishing states,
cruelty and tyranny are not necessarily involved;
when speaking of strong and well-governed states,
might and benevolence-righteousness are not necessarily involved.
If the ruler is advanced in age,
has many concubines,
few descendants,
and alienates his clan,
it is a declining state;
if the ruler favors his ministers,
ministers curry favor with the ruler,
public laws are abandoned,
and private desires prevail,
it is a chaotic state;
if the state is poor and small,
while families are wealthy and powerful,
the ruler's authority is light,
and the ministers' influence is heavy,
it is a perishing state.
For these three signs,
one need not wait for cruelty and tyranny to appear before the state weakens;
even if it is said to exist,
I would certainly call it perished.
If internally there is no exclusive favoritism,
externally no close favorites,
collateral branches flourish and multiply,
and the order between elders and juniors is not disturbed,
it is a flourishing state;
if farming and sericulture are timely,
granaries are full,
weapons and armor are sharp and strong,
and borders are well-maintained,
it is a strong state;
if superiors do not oppress their subordinates,
subordinates do not offend their superiors,
and neither oppresses nor offends the other,
then prohibitions and orders are carried out,
everyone is selfless,
and even when facing dangers and changes,
the state cannot be invaded,
it is a well-governed state.
For these three signs,
one need not wait for might and benevolence-righteousness to appear before the state strengthens;
even if it is said to be weak,
I would certainly call it surviving.
When a governing ruler rises,
there must be those he punishes first.
Those punished first
are not necessarily thieves,
nor necessarily villains.
These two evils
are great harms of the time,
but not the root of chaotic governance.
The root of chaotic governance lies in
subordinates encroaching on the authority of superiors,
ministers employing the methods of the ruler,
hearts not fearing the prohibitions of the time,
actions not conforming to the laws of the time—
this is the path to great chaos.
When Kǒng Qiū acted as the prime minister of Lǔ,
within seven days he punished Shàozhèng Mǎo.
His disciples came forward and asked:
"Shàozhèng Mǎo was a well-known figure in Lǔ;
for you, Master, to punish him first upon assuming governance—
is this not a mistake?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Sit!
I will tell you the reason.
There are five types of wickedness in a person,
and theft and illicit affairs are not among them.
First, a mind that is perceptive yet treacherous;
second, behavior that is eccentric yet stubborn;
third, speech that is false yet persuasive;
fourth, a memory that is strong yet broad;
fifth, compliance with wrongs yet glossing them over.
For these five,
if a person possesses even one,
they cannot avoid punishment by the noble man,
and Shàozhèng Mǎo possessed them all.
Thus, his dwelling could gather followers into crowds,
his speech could embellish evil and mislead the masses,
his strong memory could overturn truth and stand alone.
He was a formidable villain among petty men,
and could not be left unpunished."
Therefore, Tāng punished Yǐn Xié,
King Wén punished Pān Zhèng,
Tàigōng punished Huá Shì,
Guǎn Zhòng punished Fùlǐ Yǐ,
Zǐchǎn punished Dèng Xī and Shǐ Fù.
These six individuals,
though from different eras, shared the same mindset,
and could not be left unpunished.
The "Shī" says:
"Anxious is my heart,
vexed by the crowd of petty men."
When petty men form groups,
that is truly fearsome.
The "Yǔ" says:
"Cunning speech can delude ghosts and spirits."
It is said:
"Ghosts and spirits are intelligent and upright;
who says they can be deluded?"
The reply is:
"Even if ghosts and spirits are indeed not deluded,
this especially shows the skill of cunning speech,
which can penetrate anywhere."
Though those skilled in debate may not delude ghosts and spirits,
they clearly delude people.
This is evident.
They probe people's hearts,
measure people's desires,
comply with people's preferences,
and dare not oppose them,
leading people into evil while seeking their own gain.
People enjoy hearing their own praises,
and they are adept at promoting them;
people dislike hearing their own faults,
and they are adept at concealing them.
They grasp intentions from a glance,
and anticipate them before words and actions.
Ordinary people are pleased to hear praise
and distressed to hear criticism—
this is the general sentiment of the masses.
They are happy with those who agree with them
and angered by those who disagree—
this is the common sentiment of people.
Therefore, cunning people are skilled at praising,
skilled at compliance;
if others say yes,
they also say yes;
if others say no,
they also say no.
They follow what others love,
and join in what others hate.
Thus, even if an enlightened ruler can accept the upright,
he may not necessarily be close to them;
even if he can keep cunning people at a distance,
he may not necessarily alienate them.
Therefore, Shùn and Yǔ were able to not employ cunning people,
but did not necessarily hate them.
It is said:
"Cunning speech deludes things."
That Shùn and Yǔ could not bring themselves to hate them
must be carefully considered.
The "Yǔ" says:
"I hate purple for displacing vermilion,
and I hate glib tongues that overturn states and families."
These words are truly fearsome,
yet some never realize it in their lifetime,
with peril and ruin following closely.
The "Lǎozǐ" says:
"Govern the state with correctness,
use the military with surprise,
and win the world through non-interference."
Governance refers to names and laws.
Governing with names and laws
ensures nothing can bring chaos.
Surprise refers to strategy and tactics.
Using strategy and tactics in the military
ensures nothing can oppose it.
Whenever one can use names, laws, strategy, and tactics to correct and suppress cruel and violent tendencies,
then one has no need for action.
Having no need for action,
one gains the world.
Therefore, when governance fails, rely on laws;
when laws fail, rely on the military—
all to achieve non-interference,
not to seek strength.
Seeking strength,
the soft may instead overcome it.
The "Lǎozǐ" says:
"If the people do not fear death,
how can they be threatened with death?"
Whenever the people do not fear death,
it is due to excessive punishments.
When punishments are excessive,
the people have no reliance on life.
Having no reliance on life,
they regard the ruler's authority as insignificant.
When punishments are appropriate,
the people fear death.
Fearing death
arises from the joy of life.
Knowing the joy of life,
they can be threatened with death.
This is what the ruler should uphold,
and what ministers should be cautious about.
Tiánzǐ was reading
and said:
"The era of Yáo was peaceful."
Sòngzǐ asked:
"Was it the governance of the sage that achieved this?"
Péng Méng, present there,
responded out of turn:
"It was the governance by sage laws that reached this state,
not the governance by a sage."
Sòngzǐ inquired:
"How do a sage and sage laws differ?"
Péng Méng replied:
"You confuse names greatly!
A sage arises from oneself,
while sage laws arise from principle.
Principle emanates from the self,
but the self is not principle.
The self can produce principle,
yet principle is not the self.
Thus, the governance by a sage
is solitary rule;
the governance by sage laws,
however, leaves nothing ungoverned.
This benefits all generations,
and only a sage can encompass it."
Sòngzǐ remained puzzled,
and questioned Tiánzǐ about it.
Tiánzǐ said:
"Méng's words are correct."
An elder from Zhuānglǐ
named his elder son 'Robber'
and his younger son 'Assailant'.
When Robber went out,
his father chased after him, shouting,
saying:
"Robber!
Robber!"
The officials heard this
and bound him.
His father called Assailant to explain to the officials,
but in haste, his words didn't come out right,
only saying "Assailant!
Assailant!"
The officials thus assaulted him,
nearly killing him.
Another elder from Jìngkāngqú
named his servant 'Good Ox-killer',
and his dog 'Good Biter',
so no guest passed his gate for three years.
The elder found it strange and asked about it,
and people told him the truth.
Thereupon, he changed the names,
and guests came and went again.
The people of Zhèng called uncut jade 'pú',
while the people of Zhōu called un-dried mice 'pú'.
A man from Zhōu, carrying his 'pú',
asked a Zhèng merchant:
"Do you want to buy pú?"
The Zhèng merchant replied:
"I do."
When he produced his pú,
it turned out to be a mouse.
He then declined to take it.
Tiánzǐ said:
"People all act for themselves and cannot act for others,
so a ruler in employing people
makes them act for their own use,
not for the ruler's use."
A scholar from Jìxià commented:
"Excellent!
Tiánzǐ's words:
in ancient times, when a ruler employed ministers,
he sought not their private affection for himself,
but their manifest loyalty;
thus, those in office were necessarily capable,
and those in battle were necessarily brave.
Encouraged by salaries and rewards,
aligned by reputation and laws,
it did not stem from the ruler's personal heart,
nor benefit his own person.
As the saying goes:
'With meager pay, one cannot be entrusted to quell chaos;
with light rewards, one cannot be relied on to face hardship.'
This is what those in high position should be cautious about."
Between father and son,
some orders are necessarily followed,
and some are necessarily not.
"Divorce your noble wife,
sell your beloved concubine"
—such orders will be followed;
but if he adds:
"You dare not resent!
You dare not long!"
Such orders will not be followed.
Therefore, those in authority
must be cautious about their orders.
Generally, when people are wealthy, they do not envy official ranks and salaries;
when poor, they do not fear punishments.
Not envying ranks and salaries
means they are self-sufficient.
Not fearing punishments
means they do not rely on preserving their lives.
Both are serious issues for the state,
and if the method to prevent them is unknown,
then orders are not followed and prohibitions not heeded.
If orders are not followed and prohibitions not heeded,
there is no way to govern.
Without governance,
the ruler merely presides emptily over the state,
ruling his people in vain,
and danger and chaos can be expected imminently.
Now, if wealth comes only through ranks and salaries,
then people will strive to exert their efforts for their ruler;
if poverty results from punishments,
then all will fear crime and follow goodness.
Therefore, those who governed in ancient times
did not let people become poor or rich on their own.
When poverty and wealth both come from the ruler,
then the ruler holds exclusive control,
and the people know where to turn.
Being poor, one resents others;
being lowly, one resents the times;
yet none blame themselves—
this is the general tendency of human nature.
However, one cannot
uniformly condemn this as the general tendency of human nature.
There are also those deserving sympathy,
and this cannot be overlooked.
If calculations are equal,
yet others are rich and I am poor,
it would be admirable not to resent,
but even with resentment, there is no fault.
With equal talent and wisdom,
yet others are noble and I am lowly,
it would be admirable not to resent,
but even with resentment, there is no fault.
The flaw lies in not understanding the differences in wielding power and leveraging position,
while claiming identical intelligence and ability.
This is a failure of comprehension,
and even for a gentleman, it is a flaw,
yet also a gentleman's indignation.
When poor, people resent others;
when rich, they become arrogant toward others.
Those who resent others
suffer because others do not bestow favors on them.
It stems from emotions hard to pacify but uncontrollable,
and can still be forgiven.
Those who are arrogant have no suffering,
yet are arrogant without cause—
this is an emotion easily valued but not achieved,
and cannot be forgiven.
When people see the poor and lowly, they slight and distance themselves from them;
when they see the rich and noble, they respect and draw close to them.
If the poor and lowly seek bribes from oneself,
it is acceptable to distance from them;
even if they may not necessarily harm oneself, one must still distance from them,
because they possess nothing beneficial to offer.
If the rich and noble bestow gifts upon oneself,
it is acceptable to draw close to them;
even if they may not necessarily benefit oneself, one must still draw close to them,
otherwise they would not dare to be close to us.
These three aspects stand independently,
with no inherent reason for drawing close or keeping distant,
yet human nature ultimately cannot help but alter considerations based on poverty or wealth, lowliness or nobility,
hence it is called a great delusion.
Poverty, solitude, and low status,
in times of good governance are collectively pitied,
in times of chaos are collectively scorned.
Good governance does not exist solely for pitying the poor and lowly,
but this is one aspect of governance.
Chaotic times do not arise solely from scorning the poor and lowly,
but this is one aspect of chaos.
When every matter is well-governed, there is no chaos;
when there is chaos, there is no good governance.
Observe the prosperity of the Xià and Shāng dynasties,
and the decline of the Xià and Shāng,
and this evidence is clear.
The expectations of the poor and lowly towards the rich and noble are very modest,
yet the rich and noble fail to fulfill these very modest expectations.
What the rich and noble despise,
the poor cherish;
what the noble轻视,
the lowly honor.
Yet they do not fulfill them,
because they do not share hardships and joys.
Although they do not fulfill them,
it causes no harm to matters.
Now, the expectations of the masses towards their ruler,
are like those of the poor and lowly towards the rich and noble.
What they expect,
is roughly to care for the young and old,
fairly levy taxes,
provide timely relief for hunger and cold,
alleviate their illnesses and pains,
avoid excessive rewards and punishments,
assign labor appropriately,
merely this and nothing more,
which would not harm the ruler.
Yet if not fulfilled,
it is because they do not share toils and labors.
Therefore, as a ruler,
one must share hardships and comforts with the people.
Thus, the rich and noble may not fulfill the expectations of the poor and lowly,
but a ruler must fulfill those of the masses.
Not fulfilling the masses' expectations,
then the masses will not willingly support him.
Without their willing support,
the ruler's position will be overthrown.
Nothing is more dangerous than this!
No calamity is greater than this!
Two wise men cannot command each other,
two nobles cannot oversee each other,
two eloquent speakers cannot subdue each other,
because their strength and influence are equal.
Relying solely on cleverness,
then achievements will not be accomplished;
relying solely on obscurity,
then affairs will surely be contradictory.
A balance of clarity and obscurity,
is what the multitude relies upon.
Yǐn Wénzǐ visited King Xuān of Qí,
and the king lamented the lack of worthy men in his state,
Yǐn Wénzǐ said:
"If the state were all worthy men,
who would be beneath the king?"
The king said:
"What if the state were all unworthy men,
would that be acceptable?"
Yǐn Wénzǐ said:
"If the state were all unworthy men,
who would govern the king's court?"
The king said:
"If there were neither worthy nor unworthy men,
would that be acceptable?"
Yǐn Wénzǐ said:
"Not so,
having both worthy and unworthy men,
thus the king is honored above,
and ministers are humble below,
promoting the worthy and dismissing the unworthy,
this is the reason for having hierarchy."
Those who seek through intellect and strength,
are like playing chess,
advancing, retreating, taking, and giving,
attacking, seizing, releasing, and abandoning,
all lie within one's control.
In gambling, one may fully utilize strategic blocks and openings,
finding paths of thoroughfare,
yet cannot control the size of the dice,
which depends on chance.
Yáo as the Son of Heaven,
wore no double layers of silk,
ate no varied flavors,
had earthen steps three feet high,
with thatched roofs untrimmed.
Numbers:
ten, hundred, ten thousand, hundred million.
Hundred million, ten thousand, thousand, hundred, ten,
all originate from one,
extrapolating to countless billions without error.
Before battle,
officials read declarations and oaths,
giving repeated orders and explanations,
after which,
they then engage the enemy.
Yáo's virtuous influence spread across the four seas,
his benevolence and kindness covered all living beings.
